title: Continuous Practice
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of integrating Zen principles into daily life through continuous practice, which encompasses both formal meditation and mindfulness in everyday activities. This approach is rooted in the concept of a circular path that never ends, where spiritual development is present at every stage. By focusing on how to harmonize body, mind, and spirit with the universe, we can bring balance and harmony into our lives and ultimately contribute to saving all beings by starting with ourselves.

sentences.text: Well, good evening, everybody, and welcome.
Thank you for joining us tonight.
It's good to see you.
It's good to sit together.
Tonight I'm going to talk about continuous practice.
It's a term I've always liked, and there's a lot written about it.
A little later in the talk I'm going to go over some things that Dogen had to say about it.
I always need help when I'm dealing with Dogen, so I'll be calling in Norman Fischer and some others.
But I thought I would start with my own definition of continuous practice.
For me, it has two parts.

The first part is the more formal Zen practice: sitting meditation regularly at home, attending in person, Zoom, or Zoom events as often as possible, our day-long sits, our weekend sits, our Samish and Loon Lake sesshins, attending our Monday through Thursday 7am sits and the Wednesday night sit and the Saturday morning sit.
It also means helping out with sangha events and activities, taking a role during sesshin, helping with things like finances.
Then there's doing some reading and studying of Buddhist texts.
And if you're lucky enough to find a teacher who feels like a good fit, developing and maintaining that relationship is very helpful.
Then I would say practicing with the sangha in this way, year after year after year after year.
I've found that sangha practice is the foundation for the second part of my definition of continuous practice, which is bringing Zen practice into day-to-day life as much as possible.
That means trying to pay attention throughout the day, as much as I can, trying to be mindful of speech and actions, noticing my choices and how they turn out.
It means trying to turn towards whatever's happening in my life, even if I don't like it, and trying to develop a sense of gratitude, noticing all that I receive just because I'm alive.
I just keep working on these two parts forever.
I'll never finish.
That's fine, because the work has been worthwhile.
Now I'll say a few things about what's been written about continuous practice, starting with a fascicle written by Eihei Dogen in 1242.
His imagination and vision are so wide, it's pretty amazing how he sees things.
As I said earlier, I always need help understanding Dogen, and fortunately there's a lot written about his writing.
Norman Fischer did a number of Dharma talks on Dogen's view of continuous practice.
In his first writing on continuous practice, Dogen says:
*On the great road of Buddha ancestors, there is always unsurpassable practice, continued and sustained.
It forms the circle of the way and is never cut off.
Between aspiration, practice, enlightenment and nirvana, there's not a moment's gap.
Continuous practice is the circle of the way.*
He goes on to say:
*Accordingly, by the continuous practice of all Buddhas and ancestors, your practice is actualized and your great road opens up.
By your continuous practice, the continuous practice of all Buddhas is actualized and the great road of all Buddhas opens up.
By your continuous practice creates the circle of the way.*
So Dogen refers to the great road of Buddha ancestors and the circle of the way.
The great road of practice does not have an endpoint or a destination.
It's a way to live year after year.
This road has been traveled by all Buddha ancestors, all the wise men and women of the past.
Practice isn't linear: step one, then step two, then step three.
Dogen says all the stages of practice, aspiration, practice, enlightenment and nirvana, are present at the same time.
This is an example of his wide view of reality.
In one of his talks, Norman Fischer said of this sentence, "Dogen is saying, if you enter any moment of your life with full commitment and attention, nothing is left out."
So our practice today depends on, and is a reflection of, the Buddha ancestors of the past.
The wisdom and experience they gathered and passed on is reflected in how we live our lives now.
If they hadn't walked this great road, we wouldn't be here practicing today.
Dogen is saying that we are all on this road together, ancestors and current practitioners, and we depend on each other.
In his commentary, Norman says that we can't know how connected Dogen felt to the past in 13th century Japan.

He may have felt a strong connection to Buddha and to Chinese [unclear: "and"] ancestors, certainly more than today in the West, where, according to Norman, we are so focused on today and tomorrow and we push time forward.

I can't say that I've ever felt the presence of Buddha or any other Zen ancestor, but I have definitely felt the presence and support of several of the sangha members that I've been sitting with for so many years: sangha members from Mountain Rain in Vancouver, here at Red Cedar, from Seattle Soto Zen, from Everyday Zen in California.
This presence is felt in my home practice, and it's felt during Zoom or in-person sesshin, regardless of whether these people are in the room.
It's a real source of inspiration, support, and motivation.
I love the idea of us all being on the great road together and that our practice today brings to life the work of our ancestors.
Maybe it's like whenever you turn on a light, you activate the work of Thomas Edison and all of the men and women after him who developed electric lights.
Or when we speak or write any language, we activate the work of all the people long ago who developed written and spoken language, as well as the teachers and parents who taught us.
In this way, the past and the present are always connected.
And then a last comment from Norman Fischer: "Dogen means by continuous practice, encountering the profound wisdom of the past in the present moment of this lifetime."
So now I'm going to shift gears a little bit.
I'm going to read you a short page-and-a-half talk on continuous practice that was given by Sojun Mel Weitsman in 1997.
Mel, as many of you know, was the abbot of the Berkeley Zen Center for many years.
He began practicing Zen in the 1960s and was a student of Suzuki Roshi.
He practiced for around 60 years, and as many of you also know, he was the teacher for our founding teacher, Norman Fischer.
Mel died late last year.
His talk is called "Continuous Practice, Why and How."
*Today is the sixth day of our seven-day Rohatsu sesshin.
We've been sitting zazen, doing kinhin, eating meals, cooking meals, and serving each other.
Moment after moment, we've been dealing with our silent dramas, dealing with our not-so-silent dramas, with our complaints and our doubts.
This is continuous practice, a very concentrated time of continuous practice.
During this time, two questions come up.
One is why and the other is how.
Sesshin is pretty difficult.
It's difficult to stay in our seat, dealing with painful legs, painful mind, listening to the loop of our thoughts continually going round and round.*
*It's sometimes difficult accepting the various emotions that come up.

It's difficult just settling ourselves [unclear: "on the self"] without getting caught by emotion, thought, or painful legs, without becoming attached to any nice states of mind which might occasionally appear.
This state of mind one seeks in zazen is no special state of mind.
When we first read about meditation, it's very intriguing.
We're lured into this activity, hoping to reach nirvana.
We don't understand that nirvana is the pain in our legs.
Too bad.
So it's natural to look for something special to bring home.
We sit here for a week and we say, what happened?
Nothing happened.*
*It all went by in a moment.
What did I get after seven days?
Nothing.
Just painful legs.
So the sesshin state of mind is no particular state of mind.
What we get is no special thing.
If you've got something, that might be a mistake.
Be careful.
This is seven days of letting go, seven days of dropping, seven days of non-clinging, seven days of not discriminating, seven days of allowing whatever state of mind is present to be present.
Seven days of not chasing away evil thoughts, not coveting good thoughts, not grasping wonderful states of mind, not rejecting painful states of mind, just being present with whatever is present.
That's all.*
*The most difficult thing of all is just to stay in your seat.
We're always moving around.
That's our life.
Life doesn't stand still.
We look for the next comfortable position, the next interesting thing.
It's very hard to stay where we are, to stay in one place.
So we have these two questions.
First, why do we do this?
When we start to sit, we instinctively know why.
It's beyond our reasoning, but somewhere we know.
Knowing knows.*
*When we start to reason about it, we don't know anymore.
We try to match our reasoning with our knowing, and it brings up this question, especially when we get into a difficult spot.
It's like taking a boat ride.
We know we enjoy going out in the boat, but then a big storm comes up.
Pretty soon the boat's leaning over, the sails are starting to rip, the water's coming over the gunnels, and we say, why did we ever do this?
The real question is, how do I deal with this?
How is the practice question.
Why is valid, but it's secondary to how.
Take your life, for example.
Why were you born?
It doesn't matter.*
*Here you are.
The real question is, how do I live this life?
How do I deal with this situation?
When we hold this question of how, that's continuous practice.
You can deal with why until you get tired of it, and then turn to how.
How do I do this?
That is the koan of your life.
Occasionally, someone will ask me, how can I be a good Zen student?
Invariably, I say, just keep that question.
It's a great question.
Keep that question in all your activity.*
*How do I do what's in front of me?
How do I practice moment to moment?
We're not seeking something far off.
We're seeking to know, how do I stand in this place right now?
How do I sit in this spot right now?
Totally.
This is not just about sitting zazen, but about walking, eating, moving.
How do I harmonize body and mind with the universe?
That is our practice.
When we sit, we harmonize body and mind with the universe without discriminating, without picking and choosing.
How do we harmonize the intellect with the heart?*
*Where is the center of our being?
When we find our center, our heart, then the mind is under control.
If the mind is not under control of the heart, it becomes divorced from humanity.
It begins to exaggerate its own importance and it can become what we call evil.
Comic books are the archetypal stories which represent the real battles of our time.
Batman, Superman, Spider-Man, Wonder Woman.
In comic books, there is always an evil one with a big head.
He has all the technical control at his command.*
*The hero has spiritual strength.
This battle between the head and the heart is actually the battle of our time.
Between the forces of technology, of expanding brain power, and the spirit struggling to bring these under control.
The tensions of our time arise because technology and brain power are easily cut off from the heart, from the solar plexus, from the vital center.
In comic books, the hero is always trying to keep it together.
The same battle goes on in each one of us.
How can we keep the mind, the heart, and all the other satellites in harmony?
When the mind is divorced from our vital center, it leads to cunning, to domination, and unrest.*
*The world is in a state of terrible unrest and getting worse all the time.
Zen practice is to harmonize the mind and keep it under control so that it can work in harmony with the heart and the rest of the body.
The mind should be working for humanity, not just for its own satisfaction.
We sit up straight, harmonizing all this in one act.
We don't care so much about intellectual speculation.
Instead, we care about being grounded.
Even Buddhist speculation is not so important.
Buddhist philosophy is fine if you're grounded, but the first thing is to be grounded.*
*The first order of practice is always to be grounded.
When you pick up a cup of tea, pick up the cup with both hands.
Drink the tea with no separation between you and the cup and the tea.
The cup is not an object.
The tea is not an object.
There are no objects.
When we let go of everything, no one thing stands out.
The center of your life is the center of everything.
When we sit zazen, we bring the whole world into harmony.*
*This is called saving all beings.
Even though people are still out there killing each other, the influence of your continuous practice has far-reaching effects, which you can never know.
As long as individuals are out of balance, the world will be out of balance.
In order to bring the world into balance, we start with ourselves.
This is our way of saving beings, and this is what we have been doing all week.*
So that's Sojun Mel Weitsman's take on continuous practice.
And I think that's probably enough said by me.
So why don't we do our closing chant, and then I'm...
Yeah, it looks like there'll be time for discussion if anybody has anything they want to say.
So, okay.
